newsitem.title: UK: UK's Brown makes BoE more independent.
newsitem.headline: UK's Brown makes BoE more independent.

text.p: Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown on Tuesday announced substantial moves towards independence for the Bank of England.
The central bank now has "operational responsibility" for setting interest rates to meet an inflation target laid down by the Treasury.
The move stops short of full independence for the Bank and does not comply with the Maastricht criteria because the Treasury will still determine the inflation aim.
The new monetary framework will resemble that in New Zealand, a Treasury spokeswoman said.

The Treasury said the new Labour government had inherited the existing inflation target of 2.5 percent or less and this would be formally reconfirmend in Brown's Mansion House speech scheduled for June 12.

The inflation target will be confirmed in each budget statement and the Bank will still be required to publish a quarterly inflation report to justify its monetary operations and its analysis of the economy.

It will also have to explain how it intends to meet the inflation target, the Treasury said. The legislation will provide that if "in extreme economic circumstances, the national interest demands it, the government will have the power to give instructions to the Bank on interest rates for a limited period," Brown said.
"This power is in line with practice in other countries and could only be exercised through...legislation approved by parliament," Brown said.

The government will be responsible for determining the exchange rate regime but the Bank will have its "own separate pool of foreign exchange reserves which it may use at its discretion to intervene in support of its monetary policy objective," Brown said.

If the government instructs it, the Bank will also intervene in the currency markets as the government's agent by buying or selling the government's exchange reserves, Brown said. "All such intervention will be automatically sterlised," Brown said.

Brown also confirmed that the current contracts of Bank Governor Eddie George and his deputy Howard Davies would run their course. A second deputy governor will be appointed when new legislation comes into force. Operational decisions on monetary policy will be made by a new committee comprising the Governor, the Deputy Governor and six other members.

"The decisions will be made by a vote of the committee with each member having one vote. If there is no majority, the Governor will have the final vote. The Treasury will have the right to be represented in a non-voting capacity," Brown said.
Brown said two of the committee members would take management responsibility for monetary policy and market operations respectively.

They will be appointed by the Governor, after consultation with the Chancellor, for three year terms. The remaining four members will be appointed by the Chancellor for three year terms. They will be recognised experts and will be allowed to engage in other activities which do not give rise to a conflict of interest providing they have Brown's approval.

"The intention is to move to a situation where the six members of the monetary policy committee are appointed on a rolling basis (two per year). There will be no limit to the number of terms a member can serve," Brown said.
The committee will meet on a monthly basis. A Treasury spokesman said the first meeting would be in June.
Any decisions on interest rates will be announced immediately after the Chancellor has been notified of the decision and the proceedings of the committee.
Minutes of the meeting will be released no later than six weeks after the meeting.
Brown also announced changes in the Bank's financial arrangements. He said that the Treasury would take control of the gilt market.
"The Bank's role as the government's agent for debt management, the sale of gilts, oversight of the gilts market and cash management will be transferred to the Treasury," Brown said.

Brown said the changes would enhance accountability, making the decision-making process fully transparent. The Bank of England will give evidence to parliament through the Treasury Select Committee on an enhanced basis. Until the legislation has come into force, all aspects of the new procedures for monetary policy will operate de facto, Brown said. "I am confident these arrangements will enhance the credibility of UK monetary policy," he said.

He added that the moves were in line with Labour's manifesto commitments to ensure "decision-making on monetary policy is more effective, open, accountable and free from short-term political manipulation."

The Bank of England will be accountable to the Court for its operations and finances, Brown said. He proposed the Court of the Bank be reconstituted to comprise no more than 19 members consisting of the Governor, his two deputies and 16 non-executive members.
They will be drawn widely from industry, commerce and finance.
"I intend to appoint four new non-executive members as soon as the legislation has come into force," Brown said.
-- Cheryl Juckes, London Newsroom +44-171-542 7708
